newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: US says more upbeat on global communications deal.
newsitem.headline: US says more upbeat on global communications deal.

text.p: The chairman of the U.S. Federal Communications Commission (FCC), Reed Hundt, said on Wednesday he was more optimistic that a landmark multi-billion dollar global communication services pact would be achieved.

Hundt told reporters that about 35 countries will meet in Singapore on Monday to see if they can forge a deal to liberalise world telecommunications by February 15, 1997, the deadline set by the World Trade Organisation (WTO).
The U.S. official met Singapore Communications Minister Mah Bow Tan and the chief executive of Singapore Telecommunications Ltd, Lee Hsien Yang, to discuss the potential agreement.

"I'm much more optimistic about the situation in Singapore (of reaching a WTO agreement) than I was before the talks today," Hundt said, while urging Asian countries to set aside their reservations about a deal to pry open their telecommunications markets.

"We're talking about a World Trade Organisation agreement that is unprecedented in the effects it is likely to have on economies, on societies. If we have a global information highway, it will revolutionise education and jump start world economic development," Hundt said.
The negotiations to free up telecommunications began in 1994, but failed to meet an April 1995 deadline for an agreement. The WTO extended the deadline to February.
Hundt said the United States and the European Union had come up with changes to their original offers on opening up their industries and wanted to see Asian countries match those offers.
"I do think the number of offers ought to be increased," he said. "Indonesia has made no offer. Malaysia has made no offer."
Hundt said countries in the WTO must band together to dismantle monopolies that have profited enormously from their control over the industry.
Washington has said liberalisation of the market will eventually involve more than $550 billion in total investments.
"It's about the end of monopolies," Hundt said, adding that most of the revenue in the world telecommunications industry currently go to such monopolies or dominant carriers.
Hundt arrived in Singapore on Tuesday and will fly to Indonesia later on Wednesday.
